title: Indigenous Lands Map: Territories Context
description: Explore indigenous lands and treaty context for a place with the Indigenous Lands Map — open datasets for education and awareness. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, an Australian postcode, a Canadian city and a US county each sit within indigenous nations' territories whose names predate the maps by millennia — this layer restores those names to the geography.
quick_answer: The Indigenous Lands Map adds layers from open datasets showing indigenous lands and related context for the places you search or click. It is built for education and awareness: read whose traditional territories a place lies within — an introduction to a history, not a legal register.
steps_intro: Geography has older names than the street map's. Read them with respect:

body.t: An acknowledgement that names the actual nations of the place, spelled as the datasets spell them, means something. The
answer next to it shows the layering clearly.
Classrooms use the layer to start the honest conversation: whose land, under what treaties, with what present-day presence.
Knowing a landscape's first peoples changes what a traveller sees — and which cultural centres and tours to seek out respectfully.
The layer points onward: named nations have their own governments, sites and protocols, which are the sources to follow next.

A single point can sit inside several nations' traditional territories — boundaries in this history overlap and were never the hard lines of a modern cadastre. The layer shows what the datasets carry, overlaps included.
The dataset's spellings are the nations' own where recorded — orthography here is not pedantry, it is respect encoded in the data.

faq: No — deliberately not. The map presents open-dataset context for education and awareness. Legal questions about title, treaties and rights belong to the nations' own governments and official records.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — search or click any place; your own position is never needed.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Territory records differ by dataset and by the nations' own publications; spellings and boundary renderings vary, and overlapping territories are often drawn differently by design.
Does MapBench store my browser location?
Traditional territories were not exclusive cadastral parcels — shared use, seasons and kinship made layered geographies. The data reflects that reality.
Open projects dedicated to this mapping (community and academic efforts worldwide), drawing on the nations' published information. Coverage is strongest in North America, Australia and New Zealand.
How should I use an acknowledgement?
Name the nations of the specific place, use their preferred spellings, and learn one true thing about their present-day community. Generic words are worse than none.
Where datasets record current indigenous lands and reserves, context may appear — labelled as the dataset labels it, distinct from traditional territories.
The underlying open projects accept evidence-based input; the nations' own published maps outrank everyone else's.
